Here is what I can tell you about the **record landscape** for Kenya during Wadhala Wadhala's lifetime (1888–1960), which you can use to guide your own search on FamilySearch:

---

## Kenya 1888–1960: Record Context

### Administrative History
- **1888–1895** — Imperial British East Africa Company territory
- **1895–1920** — British East Africa Protectorate
- **1920–1963** — Kenya Colony and Protectorate

Records were kept by British colonial authorities, missionary societies, and local chiefs. Coverage varies greatly by community and religion.

### Record Types to Look For on FamilySearch

| Record Type | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Civil Registration** | British authorities began registering births, marriages, and deaths; coverage was uneven and often limited to non-African populations early on |
| **Church/Mission Records** | Missionary societies (Anglican, Catholic, Methodist, etc.) kept baptism, marriage, and burial registers — often the best source for African families in this era |
| **Colonial Census / Tax Lists** | Hut tax and poll tax records sometimes list household heads |
| **Provincial / District Records** | Administrative records held at county level |

---

## What I Recommend

1. **Search FamilySearch directly** at [familysearch.org/search](https://www.familysearch.org/search) — filter by **Place: Kenya** and browse available collections.
2. I can run a **locality guide** or a **record search** for Wadhala Wadhala if you'd like — just say "search records" or "plan research" and I'll proceed through the proper workflow.
3. If you have a **project path** set up, I can log findings and build a research plan.

output.text_response:
Good — I have a clear picture of the project. Here's a focused strategy for unindexed record sets to browse next for the Flynn research:

---

## Unindexed Browse Strategy — Flynn Parentage (q_001)

### Where the research stands

Three indexed searches are done: Patrick Flynn appears in the 1850 and 1860 censuses in Thomas Flynn's Schuylkill County household, and his 1908 death certificate names Thomas Flynn as father. The active plan item still open is **Thomas Flynn's probate/will** (pli_006) — that's the natural next browse target, and it's unindexed in Schuylkill County.

---

### Priority 1 — Schuylkill County Probate / Orphans' Court records (1870–1895)

Thomas Flynn likely died sometime between the 1860 census (when Patrick was in his household) and Patrick's 1908 death. A will or letters of administration naming Patrick as an heir would clinch the parentage. FamilySearch has **digitized but unindexed** Schuylkill County probate volumes on microfilm. Look for:

- **FamilySearch image group**: Search the catalog under *Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania > Probate records*. The Orphans' Court dockets and will books from roughly 1860–1900 are the right window.
- Browse the **will book index** first (usually a separate alphabetical index volume at the front of the film set) — look for "Flynn, Thomas" and note the will book and page number before pulling the full image.

---

### Priority 2 — Schuylkill County Deed Records (1860–1880)

If Thomas Flynn owned land, deed records can establish his children as heirs or grantees and confirm the father–son relationship. Deed records for Schuylkill County are largely digitized on FamilySearch but unindexed by name.

- Catalog search: *Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania > Land records*
- Grantor/grantee index volumes (filmed separately) are alphabetical and browseable — look for Thomas Flynn in the grantor index for the 1860–1880 window, then follow the liber/page reference to the deed image.

---

### Priority 3 — Catholic Church registers, Schuylkill County parishes

The Flynns are almost certainly Irish Catholic given the name pattern and Schuylkill County coal-region context. Patrick's baptism (ca. 1845) would name his parents directly. Key parishes active by the 1840s in the region include St. Patrick's in Pottsville and St. Joseph's in Minersville.

- FamilySearch has some Pennsylvania Catholic register microfilms; check the catalog under *Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania > Church records* and also the **Diocese of Allentown** holdings.
- These are largely unindexed — browse the baptism register pages for 1843–1848 looking for a Flynn entry with a Thomas as father.

---

### Priority 4 — 1870 Census unindexed pages (as a cross-check)

The 1870 census is indexed, but if Thomas Flynn's household wasn't captured cleanly (a common transcription problem in coal-region enumeration districts), it's worth browsing the **original enumeration district pages** for the township where the family lived in 1860. This could also catch siblings born after 1860 who would corroborate the household's composition.

---

### Suggested browse order

| # | Record set | Why unindexed browse? |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Schuylkill Co. probate will books, 1860–1895 | Directly tied to open plan item pli_006; will/admin may name Patrick as son |
| 2 | Schuylkill Co. deed grantor/grantee index, 1860–1880 | Thomas as grantor could confirm family land passed to Patrick |
| 3 | Catholic baptismal registers, Pottsville & Minersville, 1843–1848 | Could name Thomas as Patrick's father directly |
| 4 | 1870 census ED pages for target township | Closes any gap if Thomas's 1870 household was mis-transcribed |

Would you like me to look up the specific FamilySearch catalog DGS numbers for the probate or church register films so you can jump straight to the right image group?

quirks: Danish military levy rolls (laegdsruller) begin in 1789 and enroll every male from early childhood under his father's name — each son's entry sits directly beneath the father's, making the rolls DIRECT parentage evidence for a male subject.
Danish naming is patronymic before ~1850: 'Mikkel Nielsen' means Mikkel son of Niels, so the father's given name is Niels — the patronymic alone does not identify which Niels.
Vital events are recorded in parish church books (kirkeboeger); baptism entries name both parents. Civil registration is much later.
The Stagstrup parish register is only ~3% name-indexed on FamilySearch — plan to browse the register images by year rather than rely on the index.

items.claim: Polly Burton (Mary A. Burton, Polley A.P. Burton) — Jahue B. Burton's wife shown in the 1850–1880 census records in Pulaski County, Kentucky — is a different person from Mary Ann Eastham, who married Ephriam Boggs in Greenup County, Kentucky on 30 January 1844. The FamilySearch profile LYYX-DS1 incorrectly merges these two distinct women.
items.notes: Primary hypothesis for q_001. The Boggs/Eastham marriage record (src_005, a_115) provides direct evidence of a separate Mary Ann Eastham who married Ephriam Boggs on 30 January 1844 in Greenup County — a woman who cannot simultaneously be Jahue Burton's wife Polly in Pulaski County. The 'Father of the Bride' Robert Eastham named in that marriage record (a_117) must have been born approximately 1795-1805 to have a daughter old enough to marry in 1844, making him too old to be the Robert Eastham Jr. (b. ~1822, Greenup County) who co-resided with the Burtons in 1850 and 1860. Four census records consistently name Jahue's wife as Mary A. or Polly Burton but never state an Eastham maiden name, providing negative evidence against the FamilySearch merger. The 1880 census image of the Burton household (log_021) documents Polley A.P. Burton's father as Virginia-born and her mother as Kentucky-born; these facts are recorded in the log entry but no formal assertions have yet been extracted from that image, so no assertion IDs for those parental birthplace facts are available here.

items.claim: Robert Eastham Jr. (b. ~1822, Greenup County, Kentucky; co-resident in the Jahue B. Burton household in Pulaski County in both the 1850 and 1860 censuses; married Margaret Rucker in Boyd County, Kentucky, 25 January 1870) is a sibling of Polley A.P. Burton (Jahue B. Burton's wife), both being children of a Virginia-born Eastham father and a Kentucky-born mother. This accounts for both Polley's possible Eastham maiden name and Robert Jr.'s persistent co-residence with the Burton family.
items.notes: Supporting hypothesis that would explain Robert Eastham Jr.'s appearance in two consecutive Burton census households while bearing a different surname. Key supporting pattern: Robert's sworn 1870 marriage bond (a_157, a_159) reports his father born in Virginia and his mother born in Kentucky. The 1880 Burton household census image (log_021) records Polley A.P. Burton's father born in Virginia and her mother born in Kentucky — an exact match with Robert's sworn self-report. However, no formal assertions have yet been extracted from log_021 for Polley's parental birthplaces; those facts exist only in the log entry notes and cannot be cited by assertion ID here. Open conflict on Robert's mother's birthplace: a_144 (Robert's 1880 census image, log_030, unknown household respondent) lists his mother as born in Virginia, directly contradicting a_159 (Robert's sworn 1870 marriage bond) which gives Kentucky. The bond is analytically superior — sworn self-report on an original document — versus a census entry from an unknown respondent with secondary knowledge. This conflict has not yet been formally registered in the conflicts[] section and remains open. NOTE on a_159 informant_bias_notes: those notes contain an error stating the conflict is with 'Polley A.P. Burton's 1880 census which shows the mother born in Virginia.' In fact the Burton 1880 census image (log_021) shows Polley's mother born in KENTUCKY. The real conflict is between Robert's own 1880 census (a_144, Virginia) and Robert's own 1870 bond (a_159, Kentucky). This error in the existing assertion should be corrected in a future assertions-only update.

args.description: Hypothesis-tracking: death record contradicts h_002 Robert Eastham marriage attribution
args.prompt:
projectPath: /tmp/eval-ut_research_gm4-0-0-9lzlx_yv
questionId: q_001

The researcher has reported a death record — no FamilySearch ARK or record ID provided — for a Robert Eastham who died in Pulaski County, Kentucky in 1861. The death record gives his birth year as approximately 1823 and names his parents as James Eastham and Elizabeth Eastham. The researcher states this Robert Eastham matches the person appearing in the two census records where he co-resided with the Jahue B. Burton household (1850 and 1860 censuses in Pulaski County).

Current hypothesis h_002 claims that Robert Eastham Jr. (b. ~1822, Greenup County, Kentucky; co-resident in the Burton household in 1850 and 1860) is a sibling of Polley A.P. Burton (Jahue's wife), and that this same Robert Eastham Jr. married Margaret Rucker in Boyd County, Kentucky on 25 January 1870. h_002 also cites Robert's 1870 marriage bond as supporting evidence (assertions a_157 and a_159), which shows his father born in Virginia and mother born in Kentucky.

The contradiction: if the researcher's reported death record is accurate — a Robert Eastham born ~1823 who co-resided with the Burton household died in Pulaski County in 1861 — then this Robert cannot be the same person who married Margaret Rucker in Boyd County in January 1870. The 1870 groom would have to be a different Robert Eastham (a relative, perhaps, or a namesake).

The new evidence also introduces previously unknown parent names: James Eastham and Elizabeth Eastham as the parents of the census co-resident Robert.

Please:
1. Update h_002 to reflect this contradiction — if the census co-resident Robert died in 1861, the 1870 marriage (a_157, a_159) cannot be attributed to him; those assertions may belong to a different Robert Eastham.
2. Note that the death record (researcher-stated, no ARK yet) introduces James and Elizabeth Eastham as the parents of the census Robert Eastham.
3. Assess whether this new information supports, contradicts, or is neutral toward h_001 (the hypothesis that the FamilySearch merger of Polly Burton with Mary Ann Eastham/Boggs is incorrect).
4. Consider whether a separate hypothesis entry is warranted for the 1870 Robert Eastham groom as a distinct individual from the census co-resident.

Do not assign any person ID in the tree to either Robert Eastham without a formal person-evidence pass. Take only what the researcher stated about the death record — no additional inferences about place of origin or relationship beyond what they said.
